source: Zhuang et al. (2026) SenseMath: Do LLMs Have Number Sense? Shortcut use, judgment and generation
finding: Close cousin of the Einstellung design, but pointing the other way: with no induced set, models default to long step-by-step computation even when a shortcut is available. Harder problems make them find shortcuts more often. When asked if a shortcut applies, they say yes to almost everything.
numbers: 4,800 items, 8 shortcut types, digit scales 2/4/8/16, matched strong/weak/control variants; 5 LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, Qwen3-30B, Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B), 72,000 inferences, greedy, max 512 tokens. Shortcut use under plain CoT on strong items at d=4: 20-39%; with a number-sense prompt 68-86% (+47 to +50 pp). At d=16 plain CoT already gives 37-59%. Accuracy gain from the prompt for GPT-4.1-mini: +1 pp at d=2, +15 pp at d=8. Applicability judgment J1: GPT-4o-mini 100% on strong items, 0% on controls; Qwen3-8B 98%/0%.
limits: No in-context method is taught first, so this is baseline shortcut underuse, not a Luchins set. Greedy decoding, 512-token cap. 8B models gain nothing from the prompt.
agent_relevance: A plain LLM may already lack the shortcut, which is why gap 1 needs a no-example control. Difficulty goes the opposite way from Bilalic: harder items raise shortcut discovery. Judging applicability is poor, so a self-check asking 'does a shortcut apply?' will say yes to everything.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute (TMLR)
finding: Longer reasoning can lower accuracy on trivially easy questions that carry distractors or a famous-puzzle framing. When a model recognises a familiar framing it applies the memorised complex solution to a trivial question, which is Einstellung-like.
numbers: Misleading Math: 2,500 questions, 500 per distractor count n=1..5, answer always 2. Claude Opus 4 falls from near 100% to about 85-90% as reasoning lengthens. DeepSeek R1 falls from 70% to 30% at 5 distractors (natural overthinking). Famous-paradox variant: 812 questions (92 no-distractor, 180 each for n=1,3,5,7); traces start with a statement that the problem resembles the Birthday Paradox. o3 improves as distractors rise (they hide the familiar framing).
quote: This problem resembles the Birthday Paradox
limits: Tasks are riddles with a trivial answer, not a trained-method design. Claude and o3 differ in failure type. Controlled-length and natural-length setups disagree in places (the R1 drop appears only in the natural setup).
agent_relevance: Supports the overthinking side of gap 3 for the case where a familiar framing triggers a memorised heavy method. More reasoning is not a de-fixation step by itself. A cue that says 'this looks like known puzzle X' should trigger an explicit check of whether X's method is needed.

source: Liao et al. (2025) Lost at the Beginning of Reasoning
finding: The first reasoning step sets the course. If it is wrong, long-CoT models rarely recover, and they keep writing as many tokens as when it was right. This is an early, observable lock-in point.
numbers: 60 AIME24/25 questions, DS-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Qwen3-8B, Claude-3.7-Sonnet thinking. Final accuracy falls by 40% on average when the first step is wrong (43% on the hardest third, 33% on the easiest third). Correlation of first-prediction correctness with final correctness r=0.60. Forced correct vs minor-perturbed incorrect first step (Table 1): DS-R1-Qwen-7B 94.8 vs 28.5; Qwen3-8B 71.4 vs 37.0; Qwen3-235B 100.0 vs 78.7; DS-R1-Qwen-32B 100.0 vs 85.8.
limits: Math with a single numeric answer. The incorrect step is injected, not naturally produced. Not a trained-set design, but it shows that an early wrong frame persists even with extra tokens.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: the first step is a cheap place to watch and to branch. Sample several first steps and keep the best by a reward model (the paper cuts inference cost by up to 70% with no accuracy loss). In the schema, generate alternative openings before committing.

source: Choi, Zhu and Li (2025) Debate or Vote: Which Yields Better Decisions in Multi-Agent LLMs?
finding: Majority voting alone accounts for most of the gain usually credited to multi-agent debate. Debate is modelled as a martingale, so it does not raise expected correctness by itself.
numbers: Seven benchmarks. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct average accuracy: single agent 0.7205; decentralized MAD T=2 0.7377, T=3 0.7112, T=5 0.7050; centralized MAD T=2 0.6551; majority voting 0.7691. Arithmetic: single 0.8140, majority 0.9900, centralized MAD 0.43-0.55.
limits: General NLP benchmarks, not fixation items. A shared bias is not removed by voting, so this does not show that voting raises the trap rate. It only shows that debate adds no expected correctness.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: on a shared-bias item, voting copies the bias and debate does not fix it. Consistent with MedEinst (consensus agents no better) but not proof. Use a role-separated check with an outside signal rather than more agreeing agents.

source: Yang et al. (2026) Precise but Uncoupled: Reviewer Precision Does Not Guarantee Critique Uptake in Multi-Agent Math Reasoning
finding: A reviewer agent can be right often and still change nothing. A planner-executor-reviewer pipeline had the more precise reviewer but lower final accuracy than broadcast discussion, because the solver rarely acted on correct critique.
numbers: 4,181 Omni-MATH problems, gpt-oss-120b actors. Reviewer precision: PER 0.861 vs broadcast 0.644. Correct critique led to an immediate answer change 33.6% of the time (PER) vs 93.5% (broadcast). Reviewer-guided repair rate 0.051 vs 0.286. PER declined to revise correct answers 92% of the time under misleading review. Gain of multi-agent over single-agent: at most about 2 pp on tiers 1-2, 10-20 pp on tiers 6-9. Forcing explicit acknowledgment lowered final accuracy.
limits: Math, one actor family. Authors call the causal reading directional. Not a fixation benchmark.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a critic only helps if its output enters the solver's working context in a form that forces a new attempt. Measure uptake, not just reviewer accuracy. Putting guidance directly in the solver context helped partly.

source: Jang et al. (2025) Reasoning Model is Stubborn: Diagnosing Instruction Overriding (ReasoningTrap) - base vs reasoning models
finding: Closest clean LLM test of 'familiar solution overrides the stated problem'. Math and puzzle items are edited so the familiar method gives the wrong answer. Reasoning-tuned models are mostly worse than their base twins on the edited items.
numbers: ConditionedMath (AIME / MATH500), p-pass@1 (correct answer and conditions perceived), 16 samples per question: Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct 59.12 / 55.95 vs QwQ-32B 49.21 / 47.64; Qwen3-32B no-think 45.14 / 50.51 vs think 33.25 / 34.60; Qwen3-235B no-think 54.72 / 60.67 vs think 49.09 / 48.63. Original unedited items for Qwen3-32B think: 75.42 (AIME), 87.98 (MATH500). Three contamination modes: interpretation overload, input distrust, partial instruction attention.
limits: Intervals are wide (about +/-6-8). Table text was scrambled for some rows, so only rows read unambiguously are quoted. Failure here is partly 'the model thinks the user made a typo'.
agent_relevance: Gap 1/3: gives a base-vs-reasoning contrast with measured rates, but with the familiar pattern coming from pretraining, not from in-context examples. Longer thinking did not protect; in these pairs it hurt.

source: Jang et al. (2025) ReasoningTrap - budget forcing and prompt hints (ablation)
finding: A generic hint ('unusual condition, do not overinterpret') raised accuracy on edited items without hurting originals. Cutting the thinking budget also raised accuracy on edited items but wrecked the unedited ones.
numbers: Qwen3-32B think, 4 samples per question. ConditionedMath AIME p-pass@1: base 33.25; Hint 1 45.30 (original AIME 81.36 vs 75.42); Hint 2 38.24; Hint 3 41.23. Budget low (2000 tokens) 53.66 but original AIME falls 75.42 to 31.09; medium 44.07 (orig 52.21); high 39.82 (orig 57.60). ConditionedMath MATH500: base 34.60; Hint 1 46.88, Hint 2 42.11, Hint 3 37.75; original MATH500 87.98 to 88.76/88.46/90.06; low budget 51.32 (orig 68.68).
limits: One model. The authors still say rigidity persisted, and that some hints hurt on some datasets. The hints name the trap, so the test is easier than a blind one.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: partial answer. A generic warning does help an LLM here (about +12 pp on both sets), unlike Wiley's human warning. A short budget is not a fix because it breaks normal items. Wording matters: Hint 1 beat Hint 3 by 4-9 pp.

source: Jang et al. (2025) ReasoningTrap - reasoning effort sweep (o4-mini)
finding: Within one model, raising reasoning effort helped on the edited items. This conflicts with the base-vs-reasoning pairs, so length alone is not the cause; training style may be.
numbers: o4-mini ConditionedMath p-pass@1: AIME low 31.25, medium 41.98, high 36.90; MATH500 low 39.06, medium 51.80, high 53.47. Pass@1 on MATH500: 26.50, 37.50, 38.50.
limits: Appendix experiment, 4 samples; AIME not monotone. One model family.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: mixed. Within one model, more effort helped on the edited items. Across models, reasoning-tuned versions did worse than base. Do not assume more tokens lowers fixation, and do not assume it raises it.

source: Jang et al. (2025) ReasoningTrap - contamination ratio as an early signal
finding: A measurable text signal of fixation exists. Split the reasoning into paragraphs, embed each, and count the share closer to the familiar original solution than to the edited one. Accuracy holds up to about 40% contamination, then drops sharply. Wrong runs get more contaminated as the trace grows.
numbers: Contamination ratio = share of reasoning paragraphs whose cosine similarity to the original (familiar) solution exceeds that to the modified one (OpenAI small embedding model). Threshold about 40% before p-pass@1 falls. Perception of the conditions is judged from the first 15 paragraphs. Reasoning models show rising contamination with length; base models show no consistent pattern.
limits: Needs the familiar solution as a reference, so it is a diagnostic on a benchmark. The paper also proposes an early detection algorithm for cases without a reference (not tested here). Correlational.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: first measured token-level fixation signal. In an agent, the reference could be the retrieved past solution: if the trace is closer to it than to the new problem's constraints for more than about 40% of paragraphs, branch or restate.

source: Wang, Panaganti and Zhou (2026) More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence
finding: Stored abstractions (rules and summaries drawn from past runs) can keep errors alive: a rule shapes the next run, and the next rule is drawn from that run. Raw trajectories did better than stored abstractions in 7 of 9 settings. Building guidance on demand and throwing it away did best.
numbers: ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld, 3 backbones, 3 seeds, held-out success at K=10 rounds, mean over 9 settings: Anti-Persistence 59.9%, trajectory memory 53.5%, abstraction memory 49.0%, joint memory 49.3%, Reflexion (best agent baseline) 52.9%. Abstraction and joint memory below trajectory memory in 7 of 9 settings. Lowest mean LLM-call cost for anti-persistence.
limits: Not an Einstellung test, and no similarity or success-count sweep. The error source is a wrong stored rule, not a correct but over-general one.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: indirect support that persistent memory can pin an agent to an earlier habit. Keep raw past cases, rebuild guidance for the task at hand, do not store the guidance. Still no measured dose-response by example similarity.

source: Chen, Bai and Yuille (2026) The Compliance Trap: How AI Agents Consume Conflicting Memory
finding: A plausible but task-wrong memory is followed at the first step about two times in three, regardless of model strength. Once followed, success falls to a low floor, so stronger agents lose more. Recovery after leaving the right path is weak.
numbers: WebArena 77-task subset, 5 models. Compliance rate at first exposed step 63-72%. Success after compliance 17-31% vs no-memory success 23-49% on the same subset. Paired damage per compliance from 2.1 pp (Gemma-4-E4B, baseline 23%) to 25.5 pp (Qwen3.5-27B, baseline 49%, CI +11.8 to +39.2). Persistent conflicting memory is the only condition that hurts every model. Cumulative first divergence 0.86-0.94 within 7-14 steps. Re-alignment after divergence 27-42% with helpful memory vs 7-15% with conflicting memory. Persistent worse than early on Qwen3.5-27B (p=0.013).
limits: Memory is injected, not retrieved by similarity. Only web agents. No sweep over similarity or number of past successes. Small n per model.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: closest agent analogue of an Einstellung source. A retrieved case that is wrong is not just ignored. Treat a retrieved solution as a hypothesis to test at step one, and re-check at every step because repeated exposure amplified the harm.

source: Sandmann, Lapuschkin and Samek (2026) The Algorithm Is Not the Behavior: Learned Priors Override Look-Ahead in Leela Chess Zero
finding: A strong neural chess engine can compute the right tactic internally and still output a different move. Correct puzzle solutions, including immediate checkmates, appear in middle layers and are overridden in the last layers by a preference for safe, quiet play.
numbers: 8,648 forgotten positions in the dataset. Among forgotten puzzles 87.3% involve a sacrifice; correct moves are forcing (76.9% checks, 78.0% captures); the model replaces them with quiet moves in 68.3% of cases; the value head scores the position after the chosen move correctly in 97.0%. Steering against the safety direction recovers 71.7% of held-out forgotten puzzles (62.4% in the general set, plus 34.4% of never-solved puzzles). Look-ahead is intact on these positions.
limits: This is a learned prior overriding a calculated move, not a familiar longer line blocking a shorter mate. The Bilalic test (shorter mate versus familiar longer mate) was still not found.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: partly answered. Engines show a failure that looks like a set effect (prior beats computed answer) but a direct smothered-mate-vs-short-mate test is missing. For an agent: a model may hold the right answer in its working and still say the habitual one; checking the final output against the intermediate work is worth a step.

source: Tsui (2026) Self-Correction Bench: the Self-Correction Blind Spot in LLMs (COLM 2026)
finding: Models fix an error when it is attributed to the user but not when the same error is attributed to themselves. A one-word continuation, Wait, closes most of the gap. This is a measured version of 'an outside check works, an inside one does not'.
numbers: 14 open-source non-reasoning models: average blind spot 64.5%. Fine-tuning on 5,306 error-correction traces cuts it by 76.0%. Appending Wait cuts it by 89.3% and raises mean accuracy by 156%. On models' own natural errors, 4.3-10.8% of missed errors are caught when shown externally. Correction markers appear 179.5% more (GSM8K-SC) and 73.6% more (PRM800K-SC) for external errors. Claude Haiku and Sonnet 4 show 52.5% and 41.4% in the table.
limits: Injected errors in math. Mostly open non-reasoning models. Not a fixation set.
agent_relevance: Gap 2/4: supports the external-check option at near-zero token cost, and a role change (present the draft as someone else's) as a de-fixation step. Pair with Huang 2024: self-correction without an outside signal does not help.

source: Caldarella et al. (2026) Thinking Past the Answer: Evaluating Harmful Overthinking in Large Reasoning Models
finding: Many models reach the right answer early and then talk themselves out of it. Stopping at the first correct prefix would beat standard reasoning, and plain early stopping does not fix this kind of harm.
numbers: Stopping at the first correct prefix beats standard reasoning by up to 21% (about 10% on average). Early stopping cuts verbose overthinking by up to 50% but the harmful-overthinking rate rose from 10.1 (full) to 18.4 (K=5) and 14.1 (K=2) in the reported setting. 4,842 harmful traces analysed; logical drift and visual reinterpretation lead. Generalises to language-only benchmarks (GPQA).
limits: Mainly multimodal benchmarks. The first correct prefix is not knowable at run time. Overthinking here is not Einstellung, but it is the MedEinst overthinking mode (22% of noticed cases).
agent_relevance: Gap 3: more length can turn a correct early answer wrong, so length is no safe de-fixation lever. Needs an outside stop signal (a checker), not just a token cap.

source: Tang et al. (2026) MemTransfer: Benchmarking Memory Beyond Matched Experience in Embodied Decision-Making
finding: Memory of past demonstrations helps when conditions match and weakens when they change. Replacing half the relevant demonstrations with other-task ones lowered success for two trajectory memories, though the paper says part of that is lost relevant experience, not interference.
numbers: 100 navigation cases, ten task types, frozen VLM policy, six memory types. One demonstration per task, matched start: Full-context 95.3%, Episodic 100.0%; both fall at a new start. Four relevant demonstrations lift Episodic by 14.3 pp; other types gain at most 1.3 pp. Summary memory keeps 39.3% of its unchanged-route success after route blocking vs Working memory 44.8%. Episodic retrieval picked other-task histories 66.9% (confusable) vs 45.5 +/- 1.5% (irrelevant) yet mean success was not lower.
limits: Embodied navigation, not reasoning. Replacement confounds interference with loss of relevant experience. No success-count sweep for a single habit.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: weak evidence. Amount and relevance of past cases changed success, and a conflicting but similar history was not clearly worse than an irrelevant one. Do not rely on this alone.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Feedback Friction: LLMs Struggle to Fully Incorporate External Feedback
finding: Even with near-perfect feedback that names the right answer, solvers keep resisting. High-confidence answers resist most. This matches how a strong prior blocks a better route.
numbers: Up to 10 feedback rounds; solvers Llama-3.3, Llama-4-Scout/Maverick, Claude 3.7 and Claude 3.7 Thinking; feedback from GPT-4.1 mini with ground truth. All models plateau below the target accuracy on nine tasks. Counterfactual arithmetic (hexadecimal): no model above 20% after 10 iterations. Llama-4-Maverick with full feedback: AIME 73.3% (+26.7 over binary feedback), GPQA 96.5% (+10.6). Over 95% of models claim to update their beliefs yet fail to. Semantic-entropy confidence predicts resistance. Progressive temperature and rejecting prior wrong answers help but do not close the gap.
limits: Feedback is stronger than any real agent would get. Counterfactual arithmetic is partly a knowledge conflict, not strict Einstellung.
agent_relevance: Gap 4/7: an outside checker is useful only if the solver can be made to leave its answer. Forcing a new sample while rejecting the old answer helps. Confidence is a usable signal of which items will resist.

source: Mehta and Datta (2026) When Agents Commit Too Soon: Diagnosing Premature Commitment in LLM Agents
finding: Hidden-state similarity across repeated runs at the same step shows when behaviour has settled. The measure detects stability, not correctness, so it cannot alone say a commitment was premature.
numbers: Llama-3.1-70B ReAct on HotpotQA: step-4 similarity vs whole-trajectory variability r=-0.35; replicated on two other models and StrategyQA. Result disappears on hard questions. A monitor built from three partial runs predicts variability with mean AUROC 0.81. A commitment prompt cut variability 28% vs a token-matched filler but not significantly vs the standard agent after correction, and did not improve accuracy.
limits: Needs hidden states and repeated runs. Shared evidence explains much of the association. Not an Einstellung benchmark.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: an agent-level early signal exists (settling by about step 4), but it does not separate right from wrong. Use it as a trigger to run a check, not as a verdict.

source: Chen et al. (2026) MedEinst - clean read of main Table 1 and ablation (arXiv HTML v1)
finding: Clean table read from the HTML version (the PDF layout was scrambled). Baseline accuracy, robust accuracy and bias trap rate for 18 systems. Reasoning-tuned models do not show a lower trap rate than the plain base. The two generic multi-agent baselines lower accuracy and cut the trap rate only slightly.
limits: Trap rate definition is taken from the paper and not rechecked against data. Version 1 of the HTML; later versions may differ.
agent_relevance: Gap 4/10: with a clean base, MDAgent and DyLAN cut base accuracy (40.25 to 29.70 and 32.11) and only lowered trap rate by 2-3 pp, while a structured evidence-audit agent raised accuracy by 29 pp and cut the trap rate by 9.7 pp. The claim that voting raises the trap rate stays unproven: the multi-agent baselines did not raise it here. Reasoning models (R1, QwQ) are not better than Qwen3-32B on trap rate.

source: Bilalic, McLeod and Gobet (2008) Why good thoughts block better ones, Cognition 108(3):652-661 (printed record check)
finding: Printed full text could not be opened: the publisher page returned 403 and the open indexes only hold the abstract and metadata. Bibliographic record confirmed through Crossref and Europe PMC.
numbers: Volume 108, issue 3, pages 652-661, published 2008-09; Crossref lists 184 citing works; PMID 18565505.
limits: Not read in full this session. Numbers in earlier files still rest on the in-press draft.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 (printed-paper half) stays open. Keep the draft numbers marked as draft-based.
